title: Thoughts on Success in the Classroom
author: Castelino, Jo
summary: Jo Castelino argues that conventional tools for defining classroom success, success criteria, WAGOLLs, WABOLLs, tell students what a finished, successful piece of work looks like, but not how to actually get there, and that this gap matters because routine perceived failure produces disengagement and low effort, while routine success builds motivation. Rather than treating success as one endpoint, she reframes it as a series of discrete "moments" scattered through a lesson, being organised, knowing routines, retrieving prior knowledge, rehearsing explanations, answering from memory or honestly looking answers up, that each need to be defined, modelled, and given feedback on individually. She illustrates the stakes with a detailed scenario of a disengaged student who copies a mini-whiteboard answer from a neighbour during a pre-requisite check; the teacher, seeing apparent universal success, wrongly assumes the prerequisite knowledge is secure and moves on, setting the student up to struggle with the new content that depends on it. Her proposed fixes target this exact failure mode: securing attention before checks, calling on students to justify answers before confirming correctness, explicitly valuing an honest "I don't know" as useful data rather than a failure, and following up with cold call later in the lesson. She concludes that building a classroom culture of honesty about what students do and don't know is what actually makes success achievable and sustainable, more than any success-criteria document could.
points: Castelino's central reframe treats classroom success as a series of discrete, definable moments throughout a lesson, not a single end-of-task judgement measured against success criteria.

Her scenario of a student copying a mini-whiteboard answer names a specific and common failure mode: a teacher reading apparent universal correctness as evidence of secured prior knowledge, when copying has actually masked a gap.
Her proposed fix, explicitly rewarding an honest "I don't know" as useful data, directly targets the incentive structure that pushes students toward copying rather than honesty.

She positions classroom culture, built through consistent modelling and feedback on these moments, as doing more work than any written success-criteria document, since criteria describe the destination but not the route.
quotes: There is a danger that she will make an incorrect meaning of the new knowledge, leading to a lack of success in the future.

These methods don’t really show students how to achieve success, just what is expected of the completed task. Imagine if we were only given a list of ingredients and a picture of the completed dish and then expected to make said dish.

The teacher assumes the class knows the answer because it appears they all got it right. As this is part of a pre-requisite check, the teacher is now making a false assumption that this bit of knowledge has been successfully retrieved.
Explain why writing a question mark on the mini-whiteboard when the student doesn’t know an answer can be useful data for them as a teacher.
We have to be careful that the culture we are building is not one where students feel the need to cheat (by copying down answers) in order to achieve well.
